newsitem.title: USA: U.S. diesel markets perk up amid talk of CARB arb.
newsitem.headline: U.S. diesel markets perk up amid talk of CARB arb.

text.p: A high premium for California-grade (CARB) diesel lifted prices in the U.S. Gulf Coast (USG) Tuesday as traders considered shipping the distillate out west.
"People are talking about how strong the (arbitrage) is," said a U.S. Gulf trader.
"I'm sure if they can cover the shipping, that's what people are trying to do," another market player said.

Differentials on USG No. 2 low sulphur "74-grade" diesel firmed 0.75 cent Tuesday, nearly erasing the sharp losses of the underlying March NYMEX heating oil contract on which USG diesel prices are based. Prompt 74-grade material changed hands at 0.25 cent over the March screen, traders said.
West Coast traders meanwhile priced CARB diesel between 85 and 87 cents Tuesday, over 20 cents higher than prompt spot 74-grade barrels at the Gulf, or about 64 cents a gallon.
California diesel prices have outpaced world markets recently, rising nine percent last week following the unexpected shutdowns of two diesel-making units.
CARB diesel, a low-sulphur, low-aromatic fuel so named because of the California Air Resources Board which mandated its use in October 1993, is probably too difficult to make for most U.S. refiners.
But a select few refineries could make the fuel if they deemed the arbitrage attractive enough.

Those include refineries in the Caribbean run by Amerada Hess Corp on St. Croix in the U.S. Virgin Islands and by Coastal Corp on the island of Aruba, as well as Valero Energy Corp's small but sophisticated refinery in Corpus Christi, Texas.
Still, there were no reliable signs any of those players were actually rushing to take advantage of the opportunity in California, created by refinery problems in the region.

Atlantic Richfield Co last week shut its 4,000 barrel-per-day (bpd) hydrocracker in Los Angeles to repair a leak, while Tosco Corp's Avon, California east of San Francisco unit remains off line for a least another two months following a fire late last month.
But with ARCO's unit back on line this week, prices have eased, traders said, and would probably squelch the prospect of future deliveries from the Gulf.
A minimum of two weeks is required to transport Gulf products through the Panama Canal to ports in California, traders said.
"In the real world, it doesn't work," said a West Coast, referring to the arbitrage, or price appeal, between the region's.
"Now that (ARCO's) back, the market's got to come off."
